tag: this machine's memory becomes a constant in the module instead of a measurement
why: L1 — the whole reason the registry asks rather than records. A typed figure is correct the day it is written and becomes a claim about hardware nobody re-measured on every day after, which is the class FU-368 names one layer along. The leg compares against what this machine reports NOW and also reads the AST, so a constant cannot hide as prose.

tag: an unmeasurable machine is reported as unable to run a tier
old:
return UNKNOWN, (
            f"this tier needs about {needs['ram_gb']} GB and this machine's memory was not measured. "
new:
return NOT_RUNNABLE, (
            f"this tier needs about {needs['ram_gb']} GB and this machine's memory was not measured. "
why: L3 — three states, and the middle one is the point. A machine nobody could measure is not a machine that cannot run something; folding UNKNOWN into NOT_RUNNABLE would retire a tier on the strength of psutil being absent.

tag: a tier that cannot run here still lists the models it would use
why: L2, and it is the item's own sentence: a surface that lists a model the machine cannot run is the same defect as a leaderboard nothing scored. The mutation is also the plausible one - showing what the tier WOULD use looks helpful right up until someone tries to use it.

tag: a not-runnable verdict drops the arithmetic and gives only a verdict
why: L2. Without the shortfall a reader cannot tell a 0.3 GB gap from a 12 GB one - the first is a machine worth upgrading and the second is a design that will never fit, and the Owner's hardware decision turns on exactly that distinction.

tag: the router returns the lowest runnable tier, so every rule below the floor is dead code
old:
order = sorted(TIERS, key=lambda k: TIERS[k]["order"], reverse=True)
    order = [n for n in order if TIERS[n]["order"] <= TIERS[want]["order"]]
why: L4 — the defect the first draft of this module actually had, restored. The deterministic floor is order 0 and always runnable, so a walk UPWARD returns it every time and the grave-domain rule, the high-risk rule and both not-runnable rules are never reached. The guard asserts every rejection kind IS reached by some request.

tag: a grave domain is routed to a model
why: L4 and L5. Money, legal, faith, medical and safety are the domains this platform already treats as grave, and a model's answer there is not routed to automatically. L5 drives it with a model AVAILABLE, so the rule is proven to be a rule rather than a consequence of having nothing to route to.

tag: a high-risk request is routed to a model
why: L4. The mutation keeps the branch, the message and the shape and only changes the value it compares against - the way a rule stops applying without anyone deleting it, and the reason the guard asserts the rejection is REACHED rather than that the code exists.

tag: the router chooses a tier that holds no resource
why: L4. A tier can be RUNNABLE on this machine and still have nothing pulled to run - which is the live state of reflex_routing whenever the local runtime is not answering. Routing to it would hand a caller a tier with nothing behind it.

tag: a runnable tier holding a resource is still not chosen, so the floor is the only answer
new:
continue
        return {
            "tier": name, "resources": t["resources"], "domain": domain, "risk": risk,
            "wanted": want, "wanted_basis": want_why,
why: L5, the other direction. No local model is reachable in this environment, so the walk always ends at the floor and a router that could NEVER choose anything else would look identical. L5 supplies a resource and requires the reflex tier to be chosen - otherwise the router is a constant with a basis attached.

tag: the surface stops naming the Owner decision it was built under
why: L6. This item is BLOCKED BY the Owner's hardware decision and was built under its stated default. A surface that reports the consequence without naming the decision leaves a reader unable to find out whether the default still stands or has been superseded.
